english: In the spring of the fourth year of the Qingli reign, Teng Zijing was demoted to be the governor of Baling Prefecture.
In the following year, the government ran smoothly and the people lived in harmony; all long-neglected undertakings were revived.
So he rebuilt Yueyang Tower, enlarged its old structure, and engraved on it the poems and fu of worthy men of the Tang and his own time.
He asked me to write an essay to commemorate this.
In my view, the finest scenery of Baling lies entirely in one thing: Lake Dongting.
It holds distant mountains in its mouth and swallows the Yangtze River, vast and mighty, boundless in every direction;
glorious in the morning sun and gloomy at dusk, its moods change in a thousand ways.
This is the grand vista of Yueyang Tower, of which former writers have given full account.
Yet, since it connects north to the Wu Gorge and south to the Xiao and Xiang rivers, demoted officials and wandering poets often gather here.
How could their feelings at the sight of these sights fail to differ?
Now when continuous drizzling rain falls month after month without clearing, when chilly winds howl angrily and muddy waves surge skyward,
when sun and stars lose their brightness and mountains vanish from sight,
when merchants and travellers cannot proceed and masts topple and oars break,
when dusk deepens into darkness and tigers roar and gibbons cry,
then, ascending this tower, one feels parted from the capital, homesick, fearful of slander and dreading mockery, sees nothing but desolation, and is stirred to the depths of sorrow.
But in the mild spring with bright sunshine, when the waves are calm and sky and water merge into one unbounded expanse of azure,
gulls and terns fly and settle, and bright-scaled fish swim to and fro;
angelica on the banks and orchids on the islets grow lush and fragrant.

And sometimes the long mist clears entirely, the bright moon shines over a thousand li, floating light leaps like gold and the still reflection sinks like a disc of jade, as fishermen's songs answer one another—such joy is boundless!
Then, ascending this tower, one feels heart opened and spirit refreshed, forgets both favour and disgrace, drinks wine facing the breeze, and is filled to overflowing with delight.
I have tried to fathom the mind of the ancient benevolent men—it may differ from both of these.
They were not glad because of external things, nor sad because of their own situation;
high at court, they worried about their people;
far away in the rivers and lakes, they worried about their ruler.
Thus in advance they worried, and in retirement they worried too.
But when, then, could they be joyful?
They would surely say: "To be the first in the world to worry, and the last in the world to rejoice."
Without such men, with whom should I associate?
Written on the fifteenth day of the ninth month of the sixth year.
All around Chu are mountains.
Its many peaks to the southwest, with woods and ravines of exceptional beauty, look lush, deep and graceful—that is Langya.
After walking six or seven li into the mountains, one gradually hears the murmuring of water gushing forth from between two peaks—that is Niang Spring.
As the path winds round the peaks, there stands a pavilion perching like a bird with spread wings above the spring—that is the Old Drunkard's Pavilion.
Who built this pavilion?
A monk of the mountain, Zhixian.
Who named it?
The governor, after himself.
The governor and his guests come here to drink; he drinks little yet soon gets drunk, and being the eldest in years, he styled himself the Old Drunkard.
The Old Drunkard's heart is not in the wine, but in the hills and streams.
The joy of mountains and waters he takes into his heart and lodges in wine.
Now, when the sun rises, the mists of the forest disperse; when clouds return, the caves grow dark—this alternation of dark and bright is morning and evening in the mountains.
Wild flowers blooming with hidden fragrance, fine trees growing luxuriant with deep shade, wind and frost lofty and pure, water fallen and rocks emerging—these are the four seasons in the mountains.
Going out at dawn and returning at dusk, the scenery of the four seasons differs, and the joy thereof is inexhaustible.

Moreover, carriers singing on the road, travellers resting under trees, those in front calling and those behind answering, old bent folk leading children by the hand, coming and going without cease—that is the people of Chu on their excursions.

Angling by the stream where the water is deep and the fish fat, brewing wine from the spring which is fragrant and the liquor clear, mountain game and wild vegetables spread in profusion before them—that is the governor's feast.

The joy of the drunken feast lies not in strings or flutes: in tosses that hit the mark, in chess games won, wine cups and tallies crossing between players, rising and sitting amid noisy cheer—that is the guests' delight.
With weathered face and white hair, slumping tipsy in their midst—that is the governor drunk.
Then the setting sun rests on the mountain, and shadows of men scatter in confusion.
The governor returns and the guests follow him.
The woods grow dark, birds chirp from above and below: the tourists are gone and the birds rejoice.
Yet the birds know only the joy of hills and woods, and know not the joy of men.
Men know the joy of following the governor on his excursions, but know not that the governor rejoices in their joy.
He who, drunk, can share their joy, and, sober, can record it in writing—that is the governor.
And who is the governor?
Ouyang Xiu of Luling.
